Milton, thanks for flying in. Before we design anything, I need to understand one thing. How do American buyers see your brand today?
Honestly? Their perception is nice Brazilian jewelry at a good price. I want to change that.
Then the first step is to stop competing on price. Luxury buyers don't want a deal. They want a story.
We have a story. My family has been making jewelry for three generations. That heritage is real.
Perfect. Telling that story is how we differentiate you from the big houses. What makes the pieces different?
The craftsmanship. Every piece is finished by hand in our workshop. We refuse to mass-produce.
Good. So I recommend positioning you in a small niche: handmade Brazilian gold for collectors. Exclusivity, not volume.
I like that. I would also like to have a tagline that people can remember.
We'll get there. First, I suggest testing two ideas with your best clients in New York. Can you send me a list by Friday?
Of course. I'm looking forward to seeing your first proposal.

Hi Milton, it's Olivia. Quick update after our meeting. I spent the weekend reading about your family's workshop, and I keep thinking about that heritage. It's the strongest thing you have, so I recommend putting it at the center of everything. My team tested two taglines with ten collectors in New York. Most of them preferred the simplest one: Made by hand. Made to last. Two people said the word Brazilian made them think of beaches, not gold, so we decided to keep it in the story and out of the tagline. One more thing. I suggest stopping the online discounts this month. You can't sell exclusivity on Monday and offer twenty percent off on Friday. That damages the perception of the brand. Let's talk on Thursday. I'm looking forward to showing you the first designs.

When a new jewelry brand contacts me, I usually avoid answering the first email. That sounds rude, I know, but I get about forty emails a week from new brands. So what makes me stop and read? Three things. First, a clear niche. If you tell me you make everything for everybody, I stop reading. Second, craftsmanship I can see. I want to touch the piece, so I expect a brand to send me a sample, not a catalog. Third, a real story. Heritage sells, but only when it's true, and my customers on Madison Avenue can tell the difference. The biggest mistake I see is brands trying to compete on price. My clients don't come to me to save money. They come to own something that nobody else has. So if you want to work with a boutique like mine, stop offering discounts and start offering a reason.
